title: Requiem in D minor
hook: The Mass for the dead Mozart was writing when he died, finished by his assistant from what he left behind.

painting.title: The Last Judgment
painting.pairingNote: Angels sound the trumpets of the Last Day and the Archangel Michael weighs the souls, the scenes of the Requiem’s “Dies irae” and “Tuba mirum”, and the Michael its Offertory prays will lead the dead into the holy light.
painting.medium: Tempera and oil on oak panel

facts: A [[requiem|requiem]] is the Catholic Mass for the dead. In the summer of 1791 a messenger brought Mozart an anonymous commission for one. It came from Count Franz von Walsegg, whose wife Anna had died that February, aged 20; the count, who was known to copy out other composers’ works and present them as his own, probably meant to do the same with this one. Mozart could only start in earnest in October, after *La clemenza di Tito*, *The Magic Flute* and the Clarinet Concerto. He fell ill in November and died on 5 December 1791, with the Requiem unfinished.

What Mozart left: the first movement, the Introitus, complete in every part. For the Kyrie, and for everything from the Dies irae to the Hostias, he wrote the voice parts and the bass line, with a few instrumental lines sketched in; the orchestra had still to be filled in. The Lacrimosa breaks off after eight bars. Of the Sanctus, Benedictus and Agnus Dei, nothing in his hand survives.

His widow, Constanze, needed the work finished to receive the rest of the fee. The composer Joseph Eybler began to complete it and gave up; Mozart’s pupil and assistant Franz Xaver Süssmayr finished the job. He orchestrated the drafts, completed the Lacrimosa and wrote the Sanctus, Benedictus and Agnus Dei, which he later claimed as his own; how much he took from lost sketches or from what Mozart told him is not known. For the last movement he brought back Mozart’s music from the Introitus and Kyrie, as Mozart had wished, according to Süssmayr and Constanze. The score went to the count with a forged Mozart signature, dated 1792.

This recording uses Süssmayr’s completion, the version performed for more than two centuries, with one addition: after the Lacrimosa, the few bars Mozart sketched for a fugue on “Amen”, played as far as he wrote them. Many stories grew around the Requiem, most of them spread by Constanze: the mysterious messenger, Mozart’s belief that he was writing it for his own funeral, his fear of having been poisoned. They are told as legends; there is no evidence for any of them.
bigPicture.inOneLine: rest and mercy (I–II), the Last Judgment in six scenes, from terror to tears (III–VIII), the Offertory (IX–X), Süssmayr’s Sanctus, Benedictus and Agnus Dei (XI–XIII), and a last light to Mozart’s own opening music (XIV).

movements.heading: Introitus: Requiem aeternam
movements.title: Introitus: Requiem aeternam
movements.summary: “Grant them eternal rest, Lord, and let perpetual light shine on them.” The only movement Mozart finished completely, every note of the orchestra in his hand. It begins with dark woodwinds alone, then trombones, then the choir, and ends on a chord that waits for an answer.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow line that sinks and rises by small steps, passed between overlapping voices. It is modelled on Handel’s funeral anthem for Queen Caroline (1737), and it returns, in different shapes, all through the Requiem.

mainIdeas.name: The colour
mainIdeas.description: two [[basset-horn|basset horn]]s and two bassoons, with trombones; Mozart leaves out flutes, oboes and horns.

mainIdeas.name: The soprano’s chant
mainIdeas.description: a plain melody on an old psalm tone.

stops.hear: Over soft, faltering string chords, the bassoons and then the basset horns play a slow, sighing tune, one entering after the other
stops.happening: The main theme, in imitation. The string chords fall off the beat, a [[syncopation|syncopation]] that runs through the movement

stops.hear: Trombones and trumpets break in with loud chords
stops.happening: The brass announce the choir

stops.hear: The choir’s basses begin, and the other voices follow one by one
stops.happening: “Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine” (“Grant them eternal rest, Lord”)

stops.hear: A single soprano sings a plain, chant-like melody
stops.happening: “Te decet hymnus, Deus, in Sion” (“A hymn befits you, God, in Zion”), on an old psalm tone of [[plainchant|plainchant]]

stops.hear: The choir takes up the chant tune, louder, with the orchestra pushing forward
stops.happening: “Exaudi orationem meam” (“Hear my prayer; to you all flesh shall come”)

stops.hear: The opening theme comes back in the choir, with quick running notes in the strings
stops.happening: “Requiem aeternam” again, the theme now combined with a new line

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Heavy chords, then the music stops on an open, unresolved chord
stops.happening: “Et lux perpetua luceat eis” (“and let perpetual light shine on them”). The movement does not close; the Kyrie follows straight on

notice: Remember two moments: the soprano’s plain chant at about two minutes, and the running notes around the returning theme at about three and a half. The last movement brings both back, to new words.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Raphaël Pichon and Pygmalion, a choir and orchestra on period instruments, recorded the Requiem in September 2023 in Namur, Belgium, after performing it for years, including in a staging by Romeo Castellucci at the Aix-en-Provence Festival in 2019. On the album the Requiem’s sections are tracks 4, 5, 7–9, 11–14, 16–18, 20 and 21; between them Pichon places plainchant and short sacred pieces by Mozart, from his teens to his last years. This guide follows the Requiem’s own tracks only.

movements.heading: Kyrie
movements.title: Kyrie
movements.summary: “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy.” A double [[fugue|fugue]]: two themes sung at the same time, one with a wide, painful leap, the other in quick runs. Mozart wrote all the voice parts and the bass; the orchestral parts, which mostly double the voices, were filled in by other hands soon after his death, probably in time for a memorial service on 10 December 1791.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, “Kyrie eleison”
mainIdeas.description: firm notes with a wide leap downwards.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, “Christe eleison”
mainIdeas.description: a rush of fast notes running alongside it.

stops.hear: The basses sing a firm theme with a wide leap while the altos rush along beside them
stops.happening: The two themes together: “Kyrie eleison” and “Christe eleison”

stops.hear: The sopranos and tenors take over the two ideas
stops.happening: The other voices enter; the fugue builds

stops.hear: The running notes climb by half-steps, and the tension rises
stops.happening: The themes in [[chromatic-scale|chromatic scale]] form, high in the sopranos

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden halt, then slow, heavy chords end on a bare, hollow sound
stops.happening: The slow ending stops on a chord without its middle note, an old-fashioned, stark close

notice: Try to hear the two themes at once: whenever one voice has the slow leap, another has the fast run.

movements.heading: Dies irae
movements.title: Dies irae
movements.summary: “Day of wrath, that day will dissolve the world in ashes.” The long medieval poem about the Last Judgment begins here, and the full choir and orchestra burst in with trumpets, drums and trembling strings. Mozart wrote the voices and the bass, with a few instrumental lines; Süssmayr filled in the rest.

mainIdeas.name: The outburst
mainIdeas.description: loud, short choral phrases over hammering brass and [[tremolo|tremolo]] strings.

mainIdeas.name: The trembling
mainIdeas.description: at the words “quantus tremor” (“what trembling”), the music itself shivers.

stops.hear: The whole choir and orchestra crash in, strings trembling, trumpets and drums hammering
stops.happening: “Dies irae, dies illa” (“Day of wrath, that day”)

stops.hear: Rising rushes in the violins; the choir climbs chord by chord
stops.happening: “Quantus tremor est futurus” (“What trembling there will be, when the judge comes”)

stops.hear: The opening outburst returns, pushed into new keys
stops.happening: The first words again, more urgent

stops.hear: The choir sings quietly in [[unison|unison]], all on the same shivering notes, then a last loud cry
stops.happening: “Quantus tremor” painted in sound, and the close

notice: The whole movement lasts about a minute and a half. Notice how rarely the strings stop trembling.

movements.heading: Tuba mirum
movements.title: Tuba mirum
movements.summary: “The trumpet, scattering its wondrous sound through the tombs of every land, will summon all before the throne.” The trumpet of the Last Day is a solo trombone: in German the same word, *Posaune*, means both. The four soloists sing in turn, from the lowest to the highest, then together. Mozart wrote the voices, the bass and the trombone solo.

mainIdeas.name: The call
mainIdeas.description: three rising notes on the trombone, answered by the bass voice.

mainIdeas.name: The four soloists
mainIdeas.description: bass, tenor, alto, soprano, each with a verse.

stops.hear: A solo trombone plays a rising call; the bass soloist answers with the same notes
stops.happening: “Tuba mirum spargens sonum” (“The trumpet, scattering its wondrous sound”)

stops.hear: The trombone keeps singing its own long line beside the voice
stops.happening: An [[obbligato|obbligato]] part for trombone

stops.hear: The tenor takes over, and the music darkens into the minor
stops.happening: “Mors stupebit et natura” (“Death and nature will be astounded”)

stops.hear: The alto, more urgent
stops.happening: “Judex ergo cum sedebit” (“When the judge takes his seat”)

stops.hear: The soprano, highest and most anxious
stops.happening: “Quid sum miser tunc dicturus?” (“What shall I, wretch, say then?”)

stops.hear: All four soloists together in short, hushed chords, answered by the strings; then a rise to the close
stops.happening: “Cum vix justus sit securus” (“when even the just are hardly safe”)

notice: Follow the order of the voices: low to high, as if the question grows more fearful with every singer.

movements.heading: Rex tremendae
movements.title: Rex tremendae
movements.summary: “King of fearful majesty, who freely saves those to be saved, save me, fount of mercy.” Only 22 bars, but full of contrast: grand, jagged rhythms for the king, then a quiet plea. Mozart wrote the voices, the bass and the first violins.

mainIdeas.name: The king
mainIdeas.description: a falling figure in sharp dotted rhythm, the old music of a royal entrance.

mainIdeas.name: “Rex!”
mainIdeas.description: the choir’s shout, placed on a weak beat, in the gaps left by the orchestra.

stops.hear: The orchestra plays a stately falling figure in sharp, jerky rhythm; the choir shouts “Rex!” in the pauses
stops.happening: “Rex tremendae majestatis” (“King of fearful majesty”)

stops.hear: The choir takes up the jagged rhythm, the voices overlapping
stops.happening: “Qui salvandos salvas gratis” (“who freely saves those to be saved”)

stops.hear: The music quietens; voices follow each other on a pleading phrase
stops.happening: “Salva me” (“save me”)

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Almost without orchestra, the choir sings softly and ends on a bare, open chord
stops.happening: “Salva me, fons pietatis” (“save me, fount of mercy”)

notice: Listen for the change from the shouted “Rex” to the whispered “salva me”. In two minutes the music goes from the throne to the person kneeling before it.

movements.heading: Recordare
movements.title: Recordare
movements.summary: “Remember, kind Jesus, that I am the reason for your journey; do not lose me on that day.” The longest movement of the Requiem, 130 bars in a gentle three-time, for the four soloists. Seven verses of the poem are sung to two themes that keep returning. Mozart wrote the voices, the bass and the orchestral links between the verses.

mainIdeas.name: The introduction
mainIdeas.description: two basset horns weaving a soft, overlapping tune over a slowly falling line in the cellos.
Theme 1, sung first by alto and bass, then by soprano and tenor.
Theme 2, “Ne me perdas”, over plain repeated chords.

stops.hear: Two basset horns weave a soft tune, one a beat behind the other, over falling scales in the cellos
stops.happening: The orchestral introduction

stops.hear: Alto and bass sing the tune together
stops.happening: “Recordare, Jesu pie” (“Remember, kind Jesus”)

stops.hear: Soprano and tenor answer, higher
stops.happening: The same theme, second pair of voices

stops.hear: A new phrase over simple, repeated chords
stops.happening: “Ne me perdas illa die” (“do not lose me on that day”)

stops.hear: The music moves into darker keys
stops.happening: “Quaerens me, sedisti lassus” (“seeking me, you sat down weary”), the middle part

stops.hear: The first theme again, now carrying the words of guilt
stops.happening: “Ingemisco, tamquam reus” (“I groan like one condemned”)

stops.hear: The opening tune returns in the home key
stops.happening: “Preces meae non sunt dignae” (“my prayers are not worthy”), the return

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The orchestra alone, falling scales, a quiet close
stops.happening: The introduction’s music ends the movement

notice: At the end of many phrases the music seems to switch from three beats to two for a moment before settling. That is a [[hemiola|hemiola]], and it gives the gentle tune a little stumble.

movements.heading: Confutatis
movements.title: Confutatis
movements.summary: “When the damned are silenced and given to the fierce flames, call me with the blessed.” Men and women answer each other: fire for the damned in the low voices, a prayer from the high ones. Then the whole choir sinks, key by key, into a hushed prayer. Mozart wrote the voices, the bass and the main violin line.

mainIdeas.name: The damned
mainIdeas.description: tenors and basses, loud, in a driving dotted rhythm over a churning bass.

mainIdeas.name: The blessed
mainIdeas.description: sopranos and altos, very soft, over gentle broken chords in the strings.

stops.hear: Tenors and basses shout over a churning, driving bass
stops.happening: “Confutatis maledictis, flammis acribus addictis” (“when the damned are silenced and given to the fierce flames”)

stops.hear: Suddenly very soft: sopranos and altos sing a gentle phrase over rippling strings
stops.happening: “Voca me cum benedictis” (“call me with the blessed”)

stops.hear: The men’s outburst again
stops.happening: The damned, a second time

stops.hear: The women’s prayer again
stops.happening: “Voca me”, a second time

stops.hear: The whole choir, very quiet; the harmony slides downwards by unexpected steps
stops.happening: “Oro supplex et acclinis, cor contritum quasi cinis” (“I pray, kneeling and bowed, my heart crushed like ashes”)

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A soft, unresolved chord hangs in the air
stops.happening: It leads into the Lacrimosa

notice: In the last part, listen to the chords sinking. Each new chord seems to go a little deeper, like someone bowing lower and lower.

movements.heading: Lacrimosa and Amen sketch
movements.title: Lacrimosa and Amen sketch
movements.summary: “Tearful will be that day, when guilty man rises from the ashes to be judged.” Mozart wrote only the first eight bars; the rest of the Lacrimosa is Süssmayr’s. Then, in this recording, a pause and something rarely heard: Mozart’s own sketch for a fugue on “Amen”, a few bars long, played as far as he wrote it.

mainIdeas.name: The rocking
mainIdeas.description: a gentle swaying rhythm of sighs in the strings.

mainIdeas.name: The climb
mainIdeas.description: the sopranos rise step by step on “resurget” (“will rise”).

mainIdeas.name: The Amen sketch
mainIdeas.description: its theme is the Requiem’s main theme turned upside down.

stops.hear: The strings sway in a gentle, rocking rhythm of sighing pairs of notes
stops.happening: The introduction, in a slow 12/8

stops.hear: The choir enters softly
stops.happening: “Lacrimosa dies illa” (“Tearful will be that day”)

stops.hear: The sopranos climb, first in short steps, then smoothly by half-steps, as the choir grows louder
stops.happening: “Qua resurget ex favilla” (“when from the ashes shall rise…”)

stops.hear: The choir reaches full strength
stops.happening: Bar 8: here Mozart’s manuscript stops. What follows is Süssmayr’s

stops.hear: Two slow, solemn chords on “Amen”
stops.happening: Süssmayr’s ending of the Lacrimosa

stops.label: Last 45 seconds
stops.hear: After a silence, voices enter one after another on a new “Amen” theme; after a few bars the music stops in mid-phrase
stops.happening: Mozart’s sketch for an Amen [[fugue|fugue]], found in Berlin in the 1960s and perhaps meant for this place

notice: Listen for the moment around the fortieth second when the choir reaches its first loud chord. That is the last bar of the Lacrimosa Mozart wrote down.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Pichon puts the Amen sketch here, at the centre of the work, as “an experience of the void” (booklet); it breaks off where Mozart’s pen stopped. Some scholars think Mozart meant the Amen fugue to end this part of the Requiem; others think it belonged to another work. Most modern completions write it out in full; Süssmayr did not use it.

movements.heading: Domine Jesu
movements.title: Domine Jesu
movements.summary: The Offertory: “Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory, free the souls of all the faithful departed from the pains of hell and from the deep pit.” Gentle and fierce by turns, with a passage for the four soloists and a choral fugue at the end. Mozart wrote the voices and the bass; Süssmayr orchestrated.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: a quiet rising figure in the strings, on the notes of a minor chord.

mainIdeas.name: The fugue “Quam olim Abrahae”
mainIdeas.description: a firm, energetic theme, passed from voice to voice.

stops.hear: Strings rise softly; the choir answers, now gentle, now forceful
stops.happening: “Domine Jesu Christe, Rex gloriae” (“Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory”)

stops.hear: Loud, sharp exclamations from the whole choir
stops.happening: “Libera eas de ore leonis” (“free them from the lion’s mouth”)

stops.hear: Voices tumble in one after another
stops.happening: “Ne absorbeat eas tartarus, ne cadant in obscurum” (“may hell not swallow them, may they not fall into darkness”)

stops.hear: Lighter: the four soloists, one after another, on the same flowing line
stops.happening: “Sed signifer sanctus Michael” (“but may Saint Michael, the standard-bearer, lead them into the holy light”), in [[canon|canon]]

stops.hear: The choir starts a fugue on a firm, striding theme
stops.happening: “Quam olim Abrahae promisisti” (“as you once promised to Abraham and his seed”)

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: The fugue ends in solid chords, in the major
stops.happening: The end of the first part of the Offertory

notice: Remember the fugue at 1:45. Mozart asked for it to be sung again at the end of the next movement.

movements.heading: Hostias
movements.title: Hostias
movements.summary: “We offer you, Lord, sacrifices and prayers of praise; receive them for the souls we remember today.” A flowing, calm movement in three-time, the most peaceful page of the Offertory. Then the “Quam olim” fugue returns, as Mozart instructed. His note “Quam olim da capo” on this page is thought to be among the last words he wrote in the score.

mainIdeas.name: The flowing hymn
mainIdeas.description: smooth choral lines in E-flat major.

mainIdeas.name: The contrast
mainIdeas.description: loud and soft exclamations in quick alternation.

stops.hear: The choir sings a smooth, flowing tune in three-time over gentle strings
stops.happening: “Hostias et preces tibi, Domine, laudis offerimus” (“we offer you, Lord, sacrifices and prayers of praise”)

stops.hear: Loud and soft exclamations alternate, wandering through many keys
stops.happening: “Tu suscipe pro animabus illis” (“receive them for those souls”)

stops.hear: A slow, creeping melody rises by half-steps, and the music turns towards the minor
stops.happening: “Fac eas, Domine, de morte transire ad vitam” (“make them, Lord, pass from death to life”)

stops.hear: The firm fugue theme of the previous movement comes back
stops.happening: “Quam olim Abrahae”, sung again note for note

notice: Listen for the words “de morte transire ad vitam”, “from death to life”. The melody creeps upwards on them, step by small step.

movements.heading: Sanctus
movements.title: Sanctus
movements.summary: “Holy, holy, holy Lord God of hosts; heaven and earth are full of your glory. Hosanna in the highest.” From here on nothing in Mozart’s hand survives: the music is Süssmayr’s. After a short, grand opening in D major, the only sharp key in the work, comes a quick fugue on “Hosanna”.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: full chords with trumpets and drums.

mainIdeas.name: The Hosanna
mainIdeas.description: a short, lively fugue in three-time with off-beat accents.

stops.hear: Bright, full chords with trumpets and drums
stops.happening: “Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Dominus Deus Sabaoth”

stops.hear: Busier lines in the strings, the choir still solemn
stops.happening: “Pleni sunt caeli et terra gloria tua” (“heaven and earth are full of your glory”)

stops.hear: Quicker, in three-time; voices enter one after another
stops.happening: “Hosanna in excelsis”, a short fugue

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: The full choir and orchestra close loudly
stops.happening: The end of the Hosanna

notice: Compare the sound with the Dies irae. The same trumpets and drums, but now in a bright major key.

movements.heading: Benedictus
movements.title: Benedictus
movements.summary: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” A long, gentle quartet for the soloists, in B-flat major, by Süssmayr; some musicians, Pichon among them, hear Mozart’s own manner in its opening. It ends with the Hosanna fugue of the Sanctus, now in a new key.

mainIdeas.name: The opening tune
mainIdeas.description: calm and singing, first in the orchestra, then in the alto and soprano.

mainIdeas.name: The wind chords
mainIdeas.description: a solemn passage in which basset horns, bassoons and trombones answer the voices.

stops.hear: The orchestra plays a calm, singing tune
stops.happening: The introduction

stops.hear: The alto takes up the tune, and the soprano soon joins
stops.happening: “Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini” (“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”)

stops.hear: A quicker, broken phrase on the same word
stops.happening: The second idea

stops.hear: Solemn wind chords answer the voices
stops.happening: The third idea, a slow, formal close of a phrase

stops.hear: The bass and then the tenor sing the opening tune
stops.happening: The first idea returns in the low voices

stops.hear: The quick Hosanna fugue returns
stops.happening: “Hosanna in excelsis”, now in B-flat major

notice: The four soloists rarely sing all at once at the start; listen for when the low voices finally take the tune.

movements.heading: Agnus Dei
movements.title: Agnus Dei
movements.summary: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant them rest.” Three times the choir calls out, and three times the music softens on “dona eis requiem”. Süssmayr wrote it, but scholars have noticed that the choir’s basses quote the Requiem’s main theme at the start, and that it resembles a passage in one of Mozart’s earlier Masses: perhaps he was following Mozart’s ideas.

mainIdeas.name: The call
mainIdeas.description: loud, chordal, over restless violins.

mainIdeas.name: The answer
mainIdeas.description: soft and calm on “dona eis requiem”.

stops.hear: Restless violins; the choir calls out loudly, all voices together
stops.happening: “Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi” (“Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world”), in [[homophony|homophony]]

stops.hear: The music turns soft and smooth
stops.happening: “Dona eis requiem” (“grant them rest”)

stops.hear: The call again, in a new key
stops.happening: The second “Agnus Dei”

stops.hear: The third call
stops.happening: The third “Agnus Dei”

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: Slow, quiet chords settle into the major
stops.happening: “Dona eis requiem sempiternam” (“grant them eternal rest”)

notice: Listen to the lowest voices of the choir in the very first call. Their line is the main theme of the Introitus.

movements.heading: Communio: Lux aeterna
movements.title: Communio: Lux aeterna
movements.summary: “Let eternal light shine on them, Lord, with your saints for ever.” For the last movement Süssmayr went back to Mozart: he set the new words to the music of the Introitus, from the soprano’s solo onwards, and of the Kyrie fugue. So the Requiem ends with Mozart’s own music.

mainIdeas.description: The soprano’s chant from the first movement, now on “Lux aeterna”.
The Kyrie fugue, now on “Cum sanctis tuis”.

stops.hear: A few bars of orchestra, then the soprano sings the plain, chant-like melody of the first movement
stops.happening: “Lux aeterna luceat eis, Domine” (“let eternal light shine on them, Lord”)

stops.hear: The choir takes up the chant tune
stops.happening: “Cum sanctis tuis in aeternum, quia pius es” (“with your saints for ever, for you are merciful”)

stops.hear: The main theme returns with the running notes in the strings
stops.happening: “Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine”

stops.hear: The two fugue themes of the Kyrie: the wide leap and the fast runs
stops.happening: “Cum sanctis tuis in aeternum”, on the Kyrie music

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden slowing, then the bare, hollow last chord
stops.happening: The same stark close as the Kyrie

notice: If you remember the Introitus and the Kyrie, this movement is a return: the same music, new words, and in the end the same hollow chord.

threads.title: Mozart and Süssmayr
threads.body: Mozart’s share is largest at the start and fades as the work goes on: complete in the Introitus, voices and bass up to the Hostias, nothing from the Sanctus. The music returns to him in the Communio.

threads.title: One theme
threads.body: The slow, step-by-step theme of the opening returns in the Kyrie, at the end of the Lacrimosa, under the Agnus Dei and in the Communio; the Amen sketch turns it upside down.

threads.title: A dark orchestra
threads.body: Basset horns, bassoons and trombones instead of flutes, oboes and horns. The trombones bring the Last Day: in the Tuba mirum one of them is the trumpet that wakes the dead.
